description_en: Ajayamerukoṭa is located approximately 4 km northwest of Amargaḍhī, which serves as the headquarters of Dadeldhura district. Many of the monuments in the area are situated on the right bank of the Chaurī Gāḍ river, which is a tributary of the Mahakali (or Sharda) river, forming the western border between India and Nepal. In the vicinity of the monument, there are other contemporary constructions such asDDL0110,DDL0111,DDL0112,DDL0113andDDL0120.The Ajayamerukoṭa area is renowned for its rich collection of monuments, primarily erected during the 14th and 15th centuries. According to D. P. Ojha, Ajayamerukoṭa served as a local capital for the Khasiya kings from Jumla, who were part of the Khaśa Malla emperors during the 12th to 14th centuries (Ojha 1989, p. 54). Around the mid-14th century, Ajayamerukoṭa gained greater prominence as the capital of the Doti kingdom, particularly during the reign of King Niraya Pāla (approximately 1362-1383 CE). It was during this period that Doti emerged as an independent entity separate from the Khaśa Malla empire. This political and economic growth is reflected in the numerous monuments constructed during the second half of the 14th century and throughout the 15th century.The monument is oriented towards the west. The door lintel features a carved relief of Gaṇeśa, indicating the temple's affiliation with the Śaiva tradition. The single sanctum room is topped by a tower structure (śikhara). The facades of the tower are adorned with carved reliefs of floral motifs, and the east side features a depiction of a devotee. However, there are no images of divinities present inside the sanctum.The monument underwent reconstruction by Nepal's Department of Archaeology, as evidenced by the inventory numbers still visible on the structure. Therefore, it is possible that some elements may have been displaced, lost, or stolen. Blocks have been carved to replace missing ones.This architectural style, featuring a central pavilion (maṇḍapa,baiṭhak) flanked by twośikharas, is rarely found in far western Nepal but can be observed at the Bhurtī Temple Complex in Dailekh district (DLK0015). However, there are structural differences between the Bhurtī and Ajayamerukoṭa monuments. In Bhurtī, the pavilion was intentionally incorporated as a planned constituent of the temples, whereas in Ajayamerukoṭa, the pavilion appears as an independent structure. This suggests that the architects in Bhurtī drew inspiration from pre-existing models, such as the Ajayamerukoṭa monuments themselves, which may have been influenced by temples in Uttarakhand.The nearbyśikhara(DDL0132) contains an inscription dated to 1373 CE (ŚS 1295) (Sharma 2012, p. 303). This indicates that the monument was most likely built during the same period, specifically during the reign of King Niraya Pāla.
references: REFERENCES Ojha, D. P. 1988. Doti Kṣetrako Itihās tathā Saṃnskrīti . Kathmandu: Sudur Paścimāncal Sāmājik Sevā tathā Anusandhān Samiti. Sharma, Dilli Raj. 2012. Heritage of Western Nepal. Art and Architecture . Kathmandu: Centre for Nepal and Asian Studies, pp. 302-304.
